newsitem.title: UK: Industry sources criticise Internet banner ads.
newsitem.headline: Industry sources criticise Internet banner ads.

text.p: The head of a medium-sized ad agency in London on Tuesday criticised many advertising "banners" on the Internet as distracting and said consumers should be offered more inticement to look at them.

"Advertising on the Internet is incredibly cluttered and rather like government health warnings on cigarette advertising or the legal small print on financial services ads. Consumers filter it out," said Hamish Pringle, chief executive of K Advertising, which is owned by Cordiant Plc.
He told Reuters, "It takes so long to get connected to the system (the Internet) that consumers don't want to waste time getting side-tracked clicking on ads."
Pringle said that if advertisers were to entice consumers to look at their ads then they should offer some reward such as entry to a free prize draw.
Banner ads -- small rectangular images that bear an advertising message and that are "hotlinked" to another Website -- have become the standard form of advertising on the Internet.
But the Daily Telegraph said on Tuesday that many banners were failing to attract Internet users' attention.
It quoted HotWired magazine as saying that Internet users two years ago were clicking on as many as 30 percent of all Internet banner ads they saw -- a so-called 30-percent "click-through rate".
But now Internet users are more saavy about advertising and are avoiding it by not clicking on banners.

The newspaper quoted Tom Bowman, commercial director of ZDNet, as saying some of the advertisers on their Website at www.zdnet.co.uk achieved click-through rates in excess of five percent, which compared well with a typical rate of response to direct mail of only two percent.
The Telegraph said that for on-line advertising to take off the banner had to be replaced by something more interesting.
It said that one alternative to banner ads is the "full screen blipvert" that flashed up between pages of editorial.
The New York-based lifestyle magazine Word.com uses this form of advertising on its Internet site at www.word.com and it claims it is far more effective than banner ads.
